CLXXXVI.
### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### On the images of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon. Chapter 45.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a hawk and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also made an image of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon, specifically a representation of a serpent between an aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>the letter Θ</gloss>. They made it when Jupiter, together with the Head <note>the Head of the Dragon, or North Node of the Moon</note>, occupied the <term>midheaven</term> <gloss>medium coeli, the highest point of the zodiac at a given time</gloss>. They affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions, and they intended to signify a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>an intermediary spirit or guiding genius</gloss> through that image. They wished to represent it through the image of a serpent: for the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all other creatures, and they honor its divine nature. This is because a sharper spirit and a more abundant fire exist in it than in other animals. This is demonstrated both by its swift movement, performed without any feet, hands, or other instruments, and because it periodically renews its age with its slough <note>original: "eximiis"—likely a typographical error for "exuviis," the cast-off skin of a serpent</note> and becomes young again. They made a similar image of the Tail <note>the Tail of the Dragon, or South Node of the Moon</note> when the Moon was eclipsed in the Tail, or was poorly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made it to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil <term>genius</term> <gloss>spirit</gloss>. A certain Hebrew had enclosed such an image in a golden and double-layered belt which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first king of Spain of that name, whether she was aware of it or ignorant <note>Agrippa refers to the legend of Peter I of Castile and Blanche of Bourbon, where a magical belt allegedly caused the king to loathe his wife</note>. When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be encircled by a serpent. Having later discovered the magical power inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Chapter 46.

They also made images in the individual <term>mansions of the Moon</term> <gloss>the twenty-eight divisions of the zodiac through which the Moon travels each month</gloss>. In the first, for the destruction of someone, they made on an iron ring the image of a black man clothed in <term>haircloth</term> <gloss>a rough garment made of goat or camel hair</gloss> and girded, throwing a small lance with his right hand. They sealed it in black wax and fumigated it with liquid <term>storax</term> <gloss>a fragrant resin from the Styrax tree</gloss> and offered prayers. In the second, against the wrath of a prince and for his reconciliation, they sealed in white wax and <term>mastic</term> <gloss>a resin from the Pistacia lentiscus tree</gloss> the image of a crowned king, and fumigated it with <term>aloeswood</term> <gloss>agarwood, a precious fragrant heartwood</gloss>. In the third, they made an image on a silver ring, whose measurement was square, and whose figure was a well-dressed woman sitting in a chair, with her right hand raised over her head. They sealed and fumigated it with musk, camphor, and <term>aromatic hoof</term> <gloss>ungula aromatica, the fragrant operculum of certain sea snails used in incense</gloss>. They asserted that this bestowed prosperity of fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for revenge, separation, enmity, and ill-will, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and they fumigated it with red myrrh and storax. In the fifth, for the favor of kings and officials and for a good reception, they sealed in silver the head of a man, and fumigated it with sandalwood. In the sixth, to place love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and fumigated them with aloeswood and amber <note>likely referring to ambergris, a rare substance used in high-quality perfumes and incense</note>. <summary>This page describes the construction and use of talismans associated with the lunar nodes and the first seven mansions of the Moon, detailing the specific materials, symbols, and rituals required for various magical aims.</summary>
